blocks.text: Gradient checkpointing reduces the memory needed to store activations during training by discarding most of them after the forward pass and recomputing them on demand during the backward pass, trading additional computation time for a substantial reduction in activation memory usage.

This topic goes deeper into gradient checkpointing specifically, building on its brief introduction in the earlier Training Large Models on Limited GPUs topic, and connecting it directly to the VRAM management picture covered earlier in this module.
1. The Memory Cost of Storing Every Activation

blocks.alt: The Memory Cost of Storing Every Activation
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472102385-233078857.png

During a normal forward pass, every layer intermediate output, its activations, gets stored in memory, since the backward pass, covered in the Causal Language Modeling Loss topic, needs those exact values to correctly compute gradients, a memory cost that grows directly with model depth and sequence length.
2. What Gradient Checkpointing Actually Does
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472102386-572822175.png

Rather than keeping every single activation, gradient checkpointing keeps only a small number of checkpoint activations at selected points throughout the network, discarding everything in between, dramatically reducing how much needs to be held in memory at any one time.
3. Recomputing Instead of Storing
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472102386-617763903.png

When the backward pass needs an activation that was not kept as a checkpoint, gradient checkpointing simply reruns the forward computation from the nearest saved checkpoint up to the needed point, recomputing that specific activation on the spot rather than having stored it the whole time.
4. The Time for Memory Tradeoff
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472102387-436160134.png

This recomputation is not free, it means some portions of the forward pass effectively run twice, once during the original forward pass and again during the backward pass when a discarded activation is needed, meaningfully increasing total computation time even as it reduces peak memory usage.
5. Choosing Which Layers to Checkpoint
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472102387-291972724.png

Checkpointing every single layer maximizes memory savings but also maximizes recomputation cost, while checkpointing only a subset of layers, spaced throughout the network, offers a middle ground, and many frameworks let this granularity be configured to match a specific memory versus speed tradeoff.

blocks.text: 6. Gradient Checkpointing Combined With Other Techniques

blocks.alt: Gradient Checkpointing Combined With Other Techniques
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472102387-340961033.png

Gradient checkpointing addresses activation memory specifically, one of the four VRAM consumers covered in the earlier VRAM Management topic, and stacking it alongside quantization, covered in the LoRA and QLoRA module, which addresses weight memory, and LoRA itself, which addresses optimizer state and gradient memory, is exactly what makes fine-tuning large models on limited hardware practically achievable.

blocks.title: This closes the loop on the VRAM Management topic
blocks.content: Recognizing that gradient checkpointing specifically targets activation memory, rather than being a generic catch all memory fix, is what lets a practitioner combine it correctly with the other techniques targeting the other three VRAM consumers.

blocks.text: 7. How Much Memory Gradient Checkpointing Actually Saves

Activation memory can grow substantially with model depth, and gradient checkpointing can reduce that specific memory consumption dramatically, often by a large factor, since only a small fraction of the total activations need to be kept in memory at any given moment rather than the full set.
8. The Speed Cost in Practice
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472102388-825498796.png

In practice, gradient checkpointing typically slows down training by a meaningful but manageable percentage, a cost most teams find well worth paying specifically when the alternative is a training run that does not fit in available memory at all, echoing the same time for memory tradeoff seen with gradient accumulation, covered in the Training Fundamentals module.
9. When Gradient Checkpointing Is Worth Enabling

Gradient checkpointing is worth enabling specifically when activation memory, rather than weight or optimizer state memory, is the binding constraint on a training run, a determination the VRAM Management topic covered how to make, and it is often unnecessary overhead if a training configuration already comfortably fits in available memory without it.
Worked Example

A team fine-tuning with a longer sequence length than usual finds their training run exceeds available memory despite already using quantization and LoRA. Diagnosing the issue using the VRAM Management framework from earlier in this module, they identify activation memory, driven by the longer sequences, as the specific bottleneck.

Enabling gradient checkpointing brings their memory usage back within budget, at the cost of a moderate increase in training time per step, a tradeoff they judge well worth making given the alternative was not being able to run the training job on their available hardware at all.
Common Mistakes

items: Enabling gradient checkpointing by default even when activation memory was never actually the binding constraint
Not accounting for the meaningful training time increase gradient checkpointing introduces when planning a training schedule
Applying gradient checkpointing to every layer when a more moderate, selected subset would have offered a better speed and memory balance
Confusing gradient checkpointing, which targets activation memory, with quantization or PEFT, which target different VRAM consumers

blocks.text: Practice

For a training configuration you have in mind, decide whether activation memory, driven by batch size and sequence length, seems likely to be the binding VRAM constraint, and if so, sketch how enabling gradient checkpointing would change your memory versus speed tradeoff.
Key Takeaway

Gradient checkpointing reduces activation memory by discarding most intermediate activations after the forward pass and recomputing them on demand during the backward pass, a time for memory tradeoff worth making specifically when activation memory is the binding constraint on a training run, and it stacks naturally alongside quantization and PEFT, which target the other VRAM consumers covered earlier in this module.
